Game teardown · 15:21 · 50 markers reviewed

Divinestead

selected · Radar

A chill, day-based incremental strategy game that turns an Age-of-Mythology-style settlement into a readable chain of adjacent buildings, passive income, job assignments, automatic expeditions, offerings, and permanent boon choices.

Age of Mythology settlement fantasy × incremental economy × objective map without army micromanagement

Why Radar selected it

≈144Reddit score captured on the creator launch post
22comments on that post, including detailed pacing and UI feedback
≈92/daysmoothed score velocity from the assumed post start; directional, not a player count

The launch post rose well beyond Reddit's default score and generated unusually specific completion reports: commenters cited reaching the demo endpoint around days 199, 282, and 299 and discussed automation, pacing, and interface clarity. The WebGL build also launched successfully in Radar's browser check.

Product reason

The game combines a familiar mythic city-builder fantasy with a low-input incremental loop, then gives stored resources an outward purpose through workers, soldiers, monster camps, offerings, and boon paths. That makes it useful both as a product signal and as a compact systems reference.

Counter-signal

All captured discussion originated from one creator post in a genre-specific community. The score is not an audience count, later-demo monotony was reported, and no independent player-origin post was verified in the snapshot.

02
Observed product

How the game actually works

The loop below is reconstructed from the recording, transcript, on-screen instructions, and marker frames. It describes causal behaviour rather than merely listing screens.

Core loop

CollectLet days resolve and accumulate wood, gold, food, and later resources.
BuildPlace unlocked structures inside the settlement's buildable area and satisfy adjacency or cost gates.
UpgradeSpend stockpiles to raise per-day production and unlock the next tutorial objective.
AssignPut gatherers or warriors onto map jobs, camps, or the divine altar.
ChooseConvert offerings into Favor, select a boon path, expand, and repeat at a larger scale.

Recorded session, in order

00:00–00:44

Title, audio/language settings, control reference, and a brief external page check establish the build and input model.

00:53–03:03

The tutorial creates the Citadel and the first production chain: Carpenter's Workshop, mine, food hut, then upgrades.

03:03–08:44

Days advance while the player repeatedly reads costs, waits for thresholds, upgrades income, and grows the settlement footprint.

08:44–10:32

Barracks unlock Jobs. Warriors are assigned to a monster camp; the fight resolves automatically on the map.

10:32–12:43

The Divine Altar takes gatherers, produces an Offering, and converts it into one point of Favor.

12:43–15:21

Four boon paths become actionable; the player unlocks a first node, resumes expansion, and discovers a Four-leaf Clover relic.

Mechanics and implementation consequences

SystemObserved behaviourRebuild implication
Day clockA visible day-progress bar resolves production in pulses.Keep simulation time explicit; every cost should be expressible in expected days.
ConstructionA bottom build bar exposes structures; placement is constrained by map space, availability, and resources.Use authored building definitions and a grid validator rather than hard-coded tutorial placement.
AdjacencyThe early workshop is requested next to the Citadel, making settlement layout part of onboarding.Store orthogonal/diagonal neighbour rules per structure and preview valid cells before click.
UpgradesBuilding panels show level, current daily output, next output, and resource costs.Make upgrade transactions atomic and derive UI text from the same economy data used by simulation.
JobsGatherers and warriors are allocated from a central panel to villages, resource sites, camps, or the altar.Represent jobs as capacity-limited assignments with duration, reward, and recall state.
CombatWarriors travel and resolve a camp encounter automatically after a visible strength comparison.A minimal deterministic battle resolver plus readable unit/projectile feedback is sufficient for the observed promise.
OfferingsGatherers staff the Divine Altar; completion awards an Offering that becomes one Favor.Keep worker commitment, progress, claim, and currency conversion as separate states.
BoonsFavor buys nodes in Expansion, Growth, Wealth, or War paths; first-row choices expose permanent modifiers or unlocks.Build this as a data-driven prerequisite graph with mutually visible branches and a clear victory dependency.
RelicsMap exploration can reveal a named relic; the recorded Four-leaf Clover grants +1 Luck.Treat relics as inventory modifiers with acquisition events and a persistent catalogue slot.

Interface feedbackWhat keeps state readable

  • Top-right day and income panel makes the simulation pulse visible at all times.
  • Ghost footprints and coloured build cells explain where a structure will land.
  • Building cards expose both the current result and the next upgrade cost, supporting wait-versus-spend decisions.
  • Tutorial banners are persistent enough to prevent losing the immediate goal, but long passive waits can make them feel static.
  • Automatic combat is legible as a map event, yet a compact forecast and post-battle ledger would make losses easier to diagnose.
  • The boon tree provides a strong long-horizon view; it should reveal downstream numerical effects before the player commits Favor.

Coverage boundaryWhat this run proves

The run covers onboarding through the first Offering, first purchased boon, an early monster camp, and one relic. It does not cover the Great Shrine, a completed boon path, prestige, or the commenters' day-199–299 endpoint. Several minutes are intentionally spent waiting for day income, which is evidence of cadence rather than missing transcript content.

Screen-by-screen product anatomy

Interface specification

A reconstruction-oriented inventory of the visible hierarchy, controls, states, interruptions, and feedback in Divinestead. It describes observed recording evidence first; recommendations are explicitly labelled.

Evidence convention. Observed means the state is visible in the reviewed session or captured UI. Implementation guidance marks a production requirement inferred from the interaction model, not a claim about unseen code.

Viewport map

World board

The isometric settlement map owns the center, with fog/terrain boundary, buildable cells, structures, units, and combat readable as one spatial layer.

Persistent economy frame

Resource counts and progression controls sit along the top; day/tick information anchors the top-right; quests and contextual objectives stay on a side rail.

Construction and metagame

A bottom building palette handles placement; clicked structures open detail cards; Relics, Boons, and Jobs open full modal systems over the map.

Overlays & interruptions

  • Settings/language sheet and early tutorial coachmarks.
  • Building context card and explicit upgrade comparison.
  • Jobs assignment/progress, camp comparison, combat result, and relic reward panels.
  • Four-column Boons tree with dependencies, costs, and Great Shrine victory objective.

Motion, VFX & feedback

  • Build ghost, valid-cell wash, placement snap, construction puff, and resource spend delta.
  • Day tick animates production/resource counters and job progress in a readable sequence.
  • Map combat uses unit motion, projectile arcs, hit flashes, health loss, and outcome banner.
  • Quest, offering/Favor, boon, and relic completions use escalating toast/burst treatments.
  • Fog/terrain boundary and newly controlled space should reveal without obscuring cell validity.

Responsive, accessibility & edge cases

  • Localize text containers for expansion; the reviewed build used Russian, while this brief translates behavior rather than treating English widths as canonical.
  • Use icons plus text/shape for resource and build states; red/green cell color alone is insufficient.
  • On narrow screens, make the economy bar horizontally scrollable and turn side rails into drawers without covering the selected build cell.
  • Define deterministic save points around day advance, job assignment, combat, boon purchase, and relic selection.
Reconstruction test. A player should be able to read the economy, place and upgrade a structure, finish the guided objectives, assign and reclaim a job, preview and resolve a camp battle, staff the altar, buy a boon, equip a relic, and trace every resource change to an on-screen cause.

05
Reconstruction blueprint

What must exist to rebuild it

A product and systems specification derived from visible behaviour—not a claim about the original source-code architecture.

State machineSession flow

  • Title → New Game / Continue / Settings; optional language and audio configuration.
  • Tutorial objective → point at a building, resource threshold, upgrade, or assignment the player must complete.
  • Day resolution → add building production, advance jobs and expeditions, then refresh affordability and quest state.
  • Build or upgrade → validate placement/cost, spend resources, create or mutate the building, then recalculate income.
  • Job assignment → reserve workers, show travel/progress, resolve reward or combat, and return surviving capacity.
  • Offering → staff altar, fill progress, claim Offering, add Favor, then unlock an eligible boon node.
  • Long objective → develop the settlement, clear enemy camps, maximise two paths, and build the Great Shrine for victory.

Input contractControls

  • WASD or arrow keys move the camera.
  • + and − control zoom.
  • Left mouse button performs all construction, upgrade, panel, job, and map actions shown in the recording.
  • The recording switched the UI to Russian; captions in this report translate the observed meaning into English.

Rules engineResolution rules

  • Resources are stockpiles plus per-day rates; a transaction cannot complete when any required stockpile is short.
  • Each production building has a level and an upgrade curve that increases its daily yield.
  • New building types enter through tutorial/progression gates, not as a fully open catalogue on day one.
  • Available workers are reduced while assigned; different jobs require gatherers or warriors and may require a minimum count.
  • Camp resolution is strength-based and automatic in the observed run; direct unit steering was not exposed.
  • Offerings and Favor form a second-order economy: production capacity is temporarily converted into permanent progression.
  • Boon paths use prerequisites and currency costs; the displayed victory condition depends on maximising two paths before constructing the Great Shrine.

ProgressionLonger-horizon structure

  • Early progression is tutorial-gated vertical production: Citadel → wood → gold → food → upgrades.
  • Mid progression adds population roles, Barracks, map jobs, camp clearance, and new resource nodes.
  • Divine progression converts gatherer time into Offerings and Favor, then unlocks global bonuses and buildings.
  • Relics provide discrete persistent modifiers discovered through map activity.
  • The visible endpoint is a Great Shrine victory after two boon paths are maximised; the recorded session did not reach it.

Required screen and interface inventory

Minimum useful data model

  • GameState: day, dayProgress, resource stockpiles, per-day totals, tutorial step, discovered map cells, victory state.
  • BuildingDefinition: id, footprint, adjacency rule, unlock condition, base cost, level curve, production type, production amount, job hooks.
  • BuildingInstance: definition id, grid position, level, enabled state, assigned workers, local progress.
  • JobDefinition: worker class, min/max workers, travel time, work time, reward, repeat behaviour, target requirements.
  • CampDefinition: position, enemy waves, strength, rewards, cleared state; CombatState stores participants and deterministic events.
  • BoonNode: path, tier, Favor cost, prerequisites, modifier or unlock payload; BoonState stores purchased node ids.
  • RelicDefinition: name, icon, acquisition source, modifier; PlayerRelics stores discovered instances.

Expanded visual walkthrough

The complete visible arc in selected frames

21 frames were selected from 50 markers. The sequence covers onboarding, interaction, progression, supporting interfaces, and the furthest state reached while leaving repetitive markers in the source recording.

07
Production sequence

Build the causal loop before content volume

Each step leaves a testable product slice and reduces the chance of reproducing the surface while missing the system that makes it work.

  1. Create the isometric/grid camera, placement preview, Citadel, and one adjacency-gated production building.
  2. Implement the day clock, stockpiles, affordability, per-day production, upgrade curves, and save/resume.
  3. Drive the first six tutorial objectives from data and validate that no sequence can soft-lock through spending.
  4. Add worker capacity, Jobs, map targets, travel/progress, and one resource expedition.
  5. Add Barracks, warrior assignment, one deterministic camp, map combat feedback, and a reward ledger.
  6. Add Divine Altar staffing, Offerings, Favor, four boon columns, prerequisites, and one functional node per path.
  7. Add relic discovery, fog/expansion, remaining buildings, content tuning, then the two-maxed-path Great Shrine victory check.

Boundaries and unresolved behaviour

Do not encode these as facts yet.
  • Exact production and upgrade formulas beyond the values visible in the first 34 recorded days.
  • Whether camp strength is a strict threshold, probabilistic forecast, or shorthand for a more detailed combat simulation.
  • Full job catalogue, worker return/death rules, repeat automation, relic pool, Luck behaviour, and late-game resource types.
  • Exact prerequisites and effects of every boon node, and whether choosing a path creates exclusions elsewhere.
  • The complete Great Shrine construction requirements and post-victory or prestige loop.
